# Getting started

## Install

```bash
npm install @demogar/mola-ui @base-ui/react
# the three faces, self-hosted
npm install @fontsource-variable/archivo @fontsource-variable/alegreya @fontsource-variable/martian-mono
```

`@base-ui/react` is a peer dependency: install it beside the package, as above, so your app and
Mola share one copy (Mola re-exports Base UI's `DirectionProvider`, which only works with one).
The package is ESM only; `require()` works too, on Node 22.12 or later.

## Import the stylesheet and the faces once

```tsx
// styles.tsx: import it once, from your app entry
import '@fontsource-variable/archivo/wdth.css' // the width axis is load-bearing
import '@fontsource-variable/alegreya/wght.css'
import '@fontsource-variable/martian-mono/wdth.css'
import '@demogar/mola-ui/styles.css'
```

Archivo must be the **`wdth`** build. Labels and headings are set on the width axis, and the
static build falls back to a normal-width face.

### What `styles.css` does to your page

`@demogar/mola-ui/styles.css` is pre-compiled. Of the utilities, it holds only the ones the
components use, and nothing from the stories. It also holds two things that apply to the **whole
document**, not only to Mola's components:

- **Tailwind's preflight**, a reset. Every element loses its margins, headings and lists lose
  their default styles, every box is `border-box`, and native buttons and inputs inherit the font.
- **Mola's base styles.** `body` gets the cloth background, the ink colour, Archivo and the body
  size. Text selection, the focus ring, list markers and the scrollbar take Mola's colours.

In a new app that is what you want. Everything is inside CSS `@layer`s, so any CSS of yours that
is not in a layer wins over it, with no `!important`.

**Adding Mola to an existing app?** Import `components.css` instead of `styles.css`:

```tsx
// existing-app.tsx: in place of styles.css
import '@demogar/mola-ui/components.css'
```

It has the same tokens and utilities, without the preflight and the document-wide base. The reset,
the focus ring and the reduced-motion rules apply only inside Mola's components (any element with
a `data-slot` attribute, and what is inside it), and the outermost component sets its own font,
size and colour. Your `body`, your headings and your native controls stay as they were. One
difference to know: the layout and typography components (Stack, Grid, Heading, Text and the
rest) render plain elements with no `data-slot`, so they keep your page's defaults. A `Heading`
keeps the margin your CSS gives an `h2`.

## Set up the app root

Three attributes on `<html>` and up to three providers around the app, once. Mola reads nothing
else from the root.

```html
<html lang="en" dir="ltr" data-density="comfortable">
```

```tsx
// main.tsx
import { StrictMode } from 'react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'
import { DirectionProvider, ToastProvider, TooltipProvider } from '@demogar/mola-ui'

import { App } from './app'

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <DirectionProvider direction="ltr">
      <ToastProvider>
        <TooltipProvider>
          <App />
        </TooltipProvider>
      </ToastProvider>
    </DirectionProvider>
  </StrictMode>,
)
```

Why each one is there:

- **Attributes on `<html>`, not on a wrapper.** Theme, density and direction are attributes, not
  React context or props. Menus, dialogs and toasts portal to `<body>`, and an attribute on
  `<html>` is the only place they inherit from. Leave `data-theme` off to follow the operating
  system, or see [Theme](#theme) to let people choose.
- **`DirectionProvider`.** `dir` mirrors the layout, but Base UI reads keyboard direction from
  React context: arrow keys in a slider, tabs or a menu, and the side a submenu opens on. Give it
  the same value as `dir`.
- **`ToastProvider`.** It renders the toast viewport, and `useToast()` reads it. Without it,
  the first `toast.success()` throws "useToastManager must be used within `<Toast.Provider>`".
- **`TooltipProvider`** (optional). Tooltips under one provider share their delay, so moving
  along a toolbar shows the next tooltip at once instead of waiting again.

## Use a component

```tsx
// rename-agent.tsx
import { Button, Field, Input } from '@demogar/mola-ui'

export function RenameAgent() {
  return (
    <form className="grid gap-4">
      <Field label="Agent name" required hint="Shown in the run log.">
        {(control) => <Input {...control} name="name" />}
      </Field>
      <Button type="submit">Save</Button>
    </form>
  )
}
```

## How to read a component page

Every component page has the same sections in the same order, so you always know where to look.

1. **Summary and status.** What the component is for, in one sentence, and its lifecycle phase:
   Experimental, Stable or Deprecated. [Versioning](https://demogar.github.io/molaui/?path=/docs/mola-ui-versioning--overview)
   says what each phase promises. Under it, the decisions behind the component.
2. **Usage.** When to use it, when not to and what to use instead, do and don't, and how to word it.
3. **Examples.** The main example with its controls, then every documented state.
4. **Accessibility.** The keys it answers to, what Mola handles and what you must still do, and
   how it is tested: what runs on every pull request, and what has not been tested yet.
5. **Related.** The components this page sends you to, and the ones that send readers here.
6. **Changes.** What changed in the component, release by release, with the pull request and the
   commit. It is read from the changelog by each commit's scope, so it appears only on components
   that have changed. [What's new](https://demogar.github.io/molaui/?path=/docs/mola-ui-what-s-new-0-6--overview) has the
   highlights of each release.

Usage comes before the examples on purpose. "Should I use this at all?" is the first question,
and the answer is often a different component. A test holds every component page to this order,
and fails a page that would leave a section empty. What the pages don't have yet is listed on
[Known gaps](https://demogar.github.io/molaui/?path=/docs/mola-ui-known-gaps--overview).

## Theme

Two themes, chosen by `color-scheme`. With no attribute the system follows the operating system;
set `data-theme` to pin one. It works on **any subtree**, so a dark preview panel inside a light
page is one attribute.

```html
<html data-theme="dark">
<section data-theme="light">…</section>
```

Re-theme a subtree with `data-theme`, not by setting `color-scheme` on it yourself. Builds that
minify with Lightning CSS (Vite's production build, and the compiled `styles.css`) rewrite `light-dark()` for browsers older
than Chrome 123 and Safari 17.5, and in that form a token only changes theme where it is declared:
on `:root` and on every `[data-theme]` element. This applies whether you use the compiled
stylesheet or `tailwind.css` in your own Tailwind build.

### Let people choose a theme

Offer three choices: System, Light and Dark. Store only an explicit choice, and for System remove
the attribute, so the page goes back to following the operating system.

```tsx
// theme-switcher.tsx
'use client'

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
import { SegmentedControl } from '@demogar/mola-ui'

type Theme = 'system' | 'light' | 'dark'

const storageKey = 'theme'

function storedTheme(): Theme {
  try {
    const value = localStorage.getItem(storageKey)
    return value === 'light' || value === 'dark' ? value : 'system'
  } catch {
    return 'system' // storage can be blocked; the page still follows the OS
  }
}

export function ThemeSwitcher() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState<Theme>('system')
  // Read after the first render: the server cannot know the choice, and
  // rendering it on the first pass would not match the server's HTML.
  useEffect(() => setTheme(storedTheme()), [])

  function choose(next: Theme) {
    setTheme(next)
    const root = document.documentElement
    if (next === 'system') delete root.dataset.theme
    else root.dataset.theme = next
    try {
      if (next === 'system') localStorage.removeItem(storageKey)
      else localStorage.setItem(storageKey, next)
    } catch {
      // the choice lasts for this page only
    }
  }

  return (
    <SegmentedControl
      aria-label="Theme"
      size="sm"
      value={theme}
      onValueChange={choose}
      options={[
        { value: 'system', label: 'System' },
        { value: 'light', label: 'Light' },
        { value: 'dark', label: 'Dark' },
      ]}
    />
  )
}
```

**No flash on load.** A stored Dark must be on `<html>` before the first paint. If React sets it,
the page paints in the system theme first and then flips. Put a small script inline in `<head>`,
before any stylesheet, so it runs while the HTML is still being parsed:

```html
<script>
  try {
    var theme = localStorage.getItem('theme')
    if (theme === 'light' || theme === 'dark') document.documentElement.dataset.theme = theme
  } catch (e) {}
</script>
```

System needs no script: with no attribute, the CSS follows the operating system before any script
runs, so only an explicit choice can flash. A server-rendered app needs the same script, and React
needs to be told that `<html>` changed before it hydrated; see [Next.js](#nextjs) below.

## Density

```html
<main data-density="compact">   <!-- data-heavy tables, logs -->
<main data-density="comfortable"> <!-- default -->
<main data-density="spacious">  <!-- forms, onboarding: the original editorial metric -->
```

Density re-scales control heights, row heights, the small end of the type scale and the spacing
unit together. No component takes a density prop.
[Spacing](https://demogar.github.io/molaui/?path=/docs/foundations-spacing--overview) lists every value each density sets, and
[Tokens](https://demogar.github.io/molaui/?path=/docs/foundations-tokens--overview) every token with its value in both themes.

## Right-to-left

Layout follows `dir`, because every component is written in logical properties. Keyboard direction
does not: Base UI reads it from React context, so arrow keys in a slider, tabs or a menu, and the
side a submenu opens on, need the provider too. Set both, once, at the root: `dir="rtl"` on
`<html>`, and `direction="rtl"` on the `DirectionProvider` in [the app root](#set-up-the-app-root).

```html
<html lang="ar" dir="rtl" data-density="comfortable">
```

`dir` belongs on `<html>`, not on a wrapper, for the same reason as the theme: menus and dialogs
portal to `<body>` and must mirror too. See Foundations / Accessibility for what changes.

## Already on Tailwind v4?

Import the un-compiled layers into your own build instead of shipping a second Tailwind:

```css
@import 'tailwindcss';
@import '@demogar/mola-ui/tailwind.css';
@source '../node_modules/@demogar/mola-ui/dist';
```

The `@source` path is relative to the CSS file that contains it, so the example is for a stylesheet
one folder below the project root (`src/app.css`). It points Tailwind at the package's compiled
JavaScript: without it Tailwind never sees the classes the components use, and they render unstyled.

Every token is then a utility in your app too: `bg-cloth-pale`, `text-ink-muted`, `shadow-cut`,
`relleno`, `cut-band band-danger`, `rule-b`, `z-(--z-popover)`.

The import also closes Tailwind's own scales where Mola has an answer: the default colour palette,
radii, shadows, blurs, easings, animations, line heights, letter spacing, font families and the
container steps above `5xl` stop compiling, so `bg-red-500` or `shadow-lg` in your app produces no
CSS. That is the point of adopting the system: one scale, not two. Spacing, font weights, the
`text-*` sizes and the `sm:` … `2xl:` breakpoints stay as Tailwind has them. An app that needs the
defaults back can import only `@demogar/mola-ui/tokens.css` and bridge the names it wants.

## React Server Components

Components can be rendered from a server component (the Next.js App Router, for example). Every
module that holds state or reads context is marked `'use client'`, so it arrives as a client
component and the rest stays on the server. One limit is React's, not ours: a function cannot be
passed from a server component to a client one. That covers event handlers such as `onClick`, and
the props that take a function: `Field`'s children (the control is a render prop), `DataTable`'s
`cell`, `Slider`'s `formatValue`. Put those in a file of your own that starts with `'use client'`:

```tsx
// agent-name-field.tsx
'use client'

import { Field, Input } from '@demogar/mola-ui'

export function AgentNameField() {
  return (
    <Field label="Agent name">
      {(control) => <Input {...control} name="name" />}
    </Field>
  )
}
```

## Next.js

In the App Router, the root layout is the app root: the faces, the stylesheet, the attributes, the
providers and the no-flash theme script all go in `app/layout.tsx`. The providers are client
components, and a server layout can render them around its children.

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import '@fontsource-variable/archivo/wdth.css'
import '@fontsource-variable/alegreya/wght.css'
import '@fontsource-variable/martian-mono/wdth.css'
import '@demogar/mola-ui/styles.css'

import type { ReactNode } from 'react'
import { DirectionProvider, ToastProvider, TooltipProvider } from '@demogar/mola-ui'

// Runs before the first paint; see "Let people choose a theme".
const themeScript = `try{var t=localStorage.getItem('theme');if(t==='light'||t==='dark')document.documentElement.dataset.theme=t}catch(e){}`

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    // The script may set data-theme before React hydrates; this tells React that is expected.
    <html lang="en" dir="ltr" data-density="comfortable" suppressHydrationWarning>
      <head>
        <script dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: themeScript }} />
      </head>
      <body>
        <DirectionProvider direction="ltr">
          <ToastProvider>
            <TooltipProvider>{children}</TooltipProvider>
          </ToastProvider>
        </DirectionProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

**Fonts with `next/font`.** The Fontsource imports above work as they are. If you would rather have
Next.js self-host and preload the faces, load them with `next/font/google`, keep the width axes,
and point Mola's font tokens at the variables it creates. The tokens name the families
(`'Archivo Variable'`), and `next/font` renames them, so without that last step the components fall
back to system fonts.

```tsx
// app/fonts.ts
import { Alegreya, Archivo, Martian_Mono } from 'next/font/google'

const archivo = Archivo({ subsets: ['latin'], axes: ['wdth'], variable: '--font-archivo' })
const alegreya = Alegreya({ subsets: ['latin'], variable: '--font-alegreya' })
const martianMono = Martian_Mono({ subsets: ['latin'], axes: ['wdth'], variable: '--font-martian-mono' })

/** Put this on `<html className={fonts}>`, in place of the three Fontsource imports. */
export const fonts = [archivo.variable, alegreya.variable, martianMono.variable].join(' ')
```

```css
/* app/globals.css, imported after the Mola stylesheet */
:root {
  --font-ui: var(--font-archivo);
  --font-display: var(--font-archivo);
  --font-text: var(--font-alegreya);
  --font-mono: var(--font-martian-mono);
}
```

## Not on React?

The components are React, but the system is not. `@demogar/mola-ui/tokens.css` is plain CSS custom
properties with no build step, and the `cloth` utilities are plain CSS under Tailwind. A Vue or
server-rendered app gets the full palette, both themes and the three densities with:

```vue
<script setup>
import '@demogar/mola-ui/tokens.css'
</script>

<template>
  <button class="mola-button" data-density="compact">Run agent</button>
</template>

<style scoped>
.mola-button {
  height: var(--control-h);
  padding-inline: var(--control-px);
  background: var(--ink);
  color: var(--on-ink);
  box-shadow: var(--cut);
}
</style>
```

## Connect an AI agent (MCP)

The package ships `mola-ui-mcp`, a read-only [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server. A
coding agent can look components up through it instead of guessing props. It answers from the
same generated manifest as these pages, for the version installed in your project. Its tools:

- `list_components` and `get_component`: props, usage, accessibility, anatomy, where it is used
  and its examples. `get_component` takes a page name ("Date picker") or an export ("IconButton"),
  and `brief: true` for only the summary, usage, props and what you must handle.
- `search`: components, patterns, tokens and rules, by name or by the job ("loading state",
  "confirm a destructive action").
- `get_tokens`: every token with its role and its value in both themes, filtered by text.
- `get_rules`: the design rules, each with its reason, and the setup.
- `get_pattern`: a whole screen, what it is built from and its states.
- `check_code`: reviews code the agent wrote (TSX, JSX or CSS) against the design rules and
  returns each finding with its line, the rule it breaks and the fix. It covers what code can
  show: a border on a control, a radius, `opacity-*` on a disabled control, hex and colour names
  that are not tokens, a token outside its scope (`text-oro`), physical `pl-`/`left-` classes, spinners, hand-rolled dialogs and menus,
  other UI libraries and imports the package does not export. An error breaks a rule; a warning is
  probably wrong but needs a reason to keep. Rules that need a reading (state in glyph, word and
  colour; label wording; approval before writes) are left to review. Code that breaks a rule on
  purpose, such as the "don't" half of an example, takes
  `// check_code: allow rule N — the reason` on the line above it; an allow without a reason is
  itself an error. The library's own source, every story and these pages are checked by the same
  code in CI.

In Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add mola-ui -- npx -y --package @demogar/mola-ui mola-ui-mcp
```

Add `--scope project` to share it through `.mcp.json`. Other clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS
Code) take the same command in their JSON config:

```text
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mola-ui": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "--package", "@demogar/mola-ui", "mola-ui-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

`npx` runs the copy in your project's `node_modules` when there is one. The MCP SDK is bundled
into the bin, so it is not a dependency of the library and your app's bundle does not change.

## Figma

`tokens/mola.tokens.json` is the same token set in the [W3C Design Tokens](https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/)
format (2025.10), both themes fully resolved — including every OKLab `color-mix()` and the
translucent colours, with their alpha. Load it with Tokens
Studio to get Figma variables that match the browser to the hex. It is generated from
`tokens.css` (`npm run tokens`) and CI fails if it is stale, so the design file cannot drift from
the code.
